DOCUMENT:
2026 Employee Engagement Survey: Results Report
People Analytics Team, Brightwell Housing Association, April 2026

1. Summary
The 2026 engagement survey ran from 2 to 20 March and 1,150 colleagues responded. The overall engagement index rose from 65 to 68, its highest level since the survey began in 2019. This report sets out results by division and theme and recommends priorities for 2026-27.

2. Method
All 1,980 employees on the payroll on 1 March were invited by email, with paper questionnaires and protected time offered to repairs operatives without regular computer access. The survey was administered by an external provider and was confidential: no results are reported for groups of fewer than ten respondents. The engagement index is the mean of six questions on pride, advocacy, intention to stay, motivation, discretionary effort and satisfaction, scaled to 0-100. The questions are unchanged from 2025, so year-on-year comparisons are like for like.

3. Response and engagement by division
Table 1. Response rates and engagement index by division
Division | Headcount 2026 | Responses 2026 | Response rate 2026 | Response rate 2025 | Engagement 2025 | Engagement 2026
Repairs and Maintenance | 820 | 254 | 31% | 64% | 58 | 63
Housing Management | 610 | 427 | 70% | 78% | 69 | 70
Customer Services | 340 | 228 | 67% | 74% | 66 | 68
Central Services | 210 | 141 | 67% | 81% | 72 | 71
Total | 1,980 | 1,050 | 53% | 72% | 65 | 68

The overall response rate fell from 72% to 53%, which remains above the 50% benchmark our provider regards as robust for organisations of our size.

Every division improved its engagement score this year. The largest gain was in Repairs and Maintenance, up five points to 63. Repairs has historically been our least engaged division, and in 2025 it was the focus of a major programme: new vans and tablets for all operatives, a revised bonus scheme and monthly team briefings led by the Director of Property. The results suggest this investment is paying off.

4. Results by theme
Table 2. Theme scores (percentage agreeing), organisation-wide
Theme | 2025 | 2026 | Change
My manager supports my development | 61% | 66% | +5
I have the tools to do my job well | 54% | 62% | +8
I understand the organisation's priorities | 70% | 72% | +2
Workload is manageable | 49% | 47% | -2
I would recommend Brightwell as a place to work | 58% | 63% | +5

Tools and equipment showed the biggest improvement of any theme, consistent with the investment in Repairs. Workload remains the weakest area and is the only theme to decline. Free-text comments on workload most often referred to vacancy cover in Housing Management, where 41 posts were vacant at the time of the survey.

5. Recommendations
5.1 Extend the Repairs model of regular director-led briefings to Housing Management and Customer Services in 2026-27, given the improvement it has delivered in Repairs.
5.2 Prioritise recruitment to Housing Management vacancies, with a target to halve the vacancy count by October.
5.3 Repeat the survey in March 2027 with the same questions and method.

6. Conclusion
2026 shows real and broad-based progress. Engagement is at its highest level since 2019, every division improved, and the division where we invested most improved most. The Executive Team can be confident that the 2025 engagement programme worked, and should extend its most effective elements across the organisation.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "The 2026 engagement survey ran from 2 to 20 March and 1,150 colleagues responded." -- The summary says 1,150 colleagues responded, but Table 1 totals 1,050 responses (254 + 427 + 228 + 141), which is also the figure consistent with the stated 53% response rate (1,050/1,980).
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Every division improved its engagement score this year." -- Table 1 shows Central Services fell from 72 to 71. Not every division improved; the claim is repeated in the conclusion.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "The largest gain was in Repairs and Maintenance, up five points to 63." -- Table 1 shows the Repairs response rate halved from 64% to 31%. With fewer than a third of Repairs staff responding, the rise could reflect who responded (e.g. disengaged staff opting out) rather than a real improvement. The report never addresses non-response bias, yet the conclusion that the Repairs programme 'worked' and should be extended depends on that division's result.

REVIEW:
# Review: 2026 Employee Engagement Survey Results Report

The report is clearly structured and the method section is good. But several of its central claims are contradicted by its own tables, and the main conclusion is weaker than the report and your description suggest. I'd fix the issues below before this goes to the Executive Team.

## 1. Factual errors to correct

**The response count is wrong in the Summary.** The Summary says 1,150 colleagues responded, and your description says "more than 1,100". Table 1 adds up to **1,050** (254 + 427 + 228 + 141), which matches the 53% response rate (1,050 / 1,980). 1,150 would be 58%.

**"Every division improved" is false.** Central Services *fell* from 72 to 71. The claim appears three times: in Section 3, the Conclusion, and your summary. Housing Management's +1 is also too small to call an improvement with confidence.

## 2. The Repairs result is the weakest part of the report, not the strongest

**Repairs response rate halved, from 64% to 31%.** This is the most important number in the report, and it gets no comment. It happened despite the paper copies and protected time, so the outreach didn't work for the group it was designed for.

- A 31% response rate is well below the provider's 50% benchmark. The organisation-wide 53% only clears the bar because other divisions carry it.
- The +5 point gain is therefore very likely to be partly or wholly selection. If less engaged operatives stopped responding, the score rises without anyone's engagement changing. The report can't distinguish the two.
- The collapse in participation may itself be an engagement signal, which points the opposite way to the headline.

**Recommendation:** Present the Repairs score as uncertain. Find out why the response rate fell, for example whether paper returns were down, whether time was actually released, or whether there was a change in survey timing relative to workload.

## 3. Part of the headline rise comes from who responded

Repairs is the lowest-scoring division. In 2026 it made up 24% of respondents, down from about 37% in 2025. Its under-representation lifts the overall average by itself. Using the report's own figures, and assuming 2025 headcounts were similar:

| Basis | 2025 | 2026 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (respondent-weighted) | 65 | 68 | +3 |
| 2026 scores at 2025 response mix | 65 | ~67.2 | ~+2 |
| Weighted by headcount | ~64.2 | ~66.9 | ~+2.6 |

There is probably a genuine rise, but roughly a third of the reported gain comes from the change in response mix. The report should show a headcount-weighted index alongside the raw one.

## 4. The tools theme doesn't support the Repairs story as written

The tools score of +8 is organisation-wide. Repairs, where the vans and tablets went, now makes up a *smaller* share of respondents than last year, so the rise can't be attributed to Repairs from this table. It may reflect other divisions, or the same response bias as above.

**Fix:** Show theme scores by division. If Repairs' tools score rose sharply, the claim stands; if not, drop it.

## 5. The causal claim and Recommendation 5.1 don't follow

Repairs received three interventions at once: vans and tablets, a revised bonus scheme, and director-led briefings. Recommendation 5.1 singles out briefings as "the improvement it has delivered", but nothing in the data separates their effects. The bonus scheme and equipment are at least as plausible drivers. Given the response-rate problem, it isn't even established that Repairs improved.

**Fix:** Reword this as "consider piloting" director-led briefings, with a way to measure their effect. Don't present it as a proven model.

## 6. The workload explanation is weaker than presented

- The link to Housing Management vacancies rests on which free-text comments were most common. Housing Management is now 41% of all respondents, the largest share, so its concerns will dominate the comments regardless of where the workload problem is worst.
- Free-text frequency suggests a link but doesn't measure a cause. Your description calls it a "specific, measurable cause", which overstates it.

**Fix:** Show the workload score by division. If Housing Management is clearly lowest, the case for 5.2 is much stronger.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Statistical noise:** Changes of ±1 to 2 points (Housing Management, Central Services, "priorities", workload) are probably within normal year-to-year variation. If the provider can supply confidence intervals or significance tests, use them.
- **Falling participation everywhere:** Every division's response rate fell, by 7 to 14 points outside Repairs. That deserves a sentence and a recommendation, since participation is often read as an engagement indicator.
- **Recommendation 5.3:** "Same method" should become "same questions, with action to restore Repairs participation". Otherwise next year's comparison will have the same problem.
- **"Highest since 2019":** No historical series is shown. Add a small trend line or footnote so readers can check it.

## Suggested revised conclusion

> Engagement rose modestly in 2026, by about 2-3 points after adjusting for response mix. Repairs and Maintenance shows the largest reported gain, but its response rate halved to 31%, so that result should be treated with caution. Response rates fell in every division and need attention before the 2027 survey. Workload remains the main concern, and Housing Management vacancies are a likely contributor.

This is still a positive message for the Executive Team. It is one that won't unravel if someone checks Table 1.
